primary_claim: Ablating a single refusal direction is no longer sufficient to remove refusal in larger/reasoning models (e.g. Qwen3 8B/14B), but ablating multiple refusal directions extracted via a cheap clustering-based method successfully reduces refusal without significantly degrading harmless-task (MMLU) performance.

effect.metric: harmfulness compliance score shift after ablating multiple refusal directions, and MMLU accuracy after ablation
effect.value: single-direction ablation insufficient for Qwen3 8B/14B (ASR can drop to 0%); multi-direction ablation shifts compliance scores higher without significant MMLU degradation (except Qwen3 14B, attributed to float16 precision)

contradicts_or_qualifies: Extends Wollschläger et al. (2025)'s gradient-based refusal-cone characterization with a cheaper (less precise) clustering-based method runnable on consumer hardware

Confirms the multi-dimensional refusal subspace found by Wollschläger et al. (2025) and Winninger et al. (2025) also applies to newer reasoning models, contradicting the earlier one-dimensional refusal-direction hypothesis of Arditi et al. (2024)
limitations_stated: The clustering-based method for extracting refusal directions doesn't guarantee full coverage of the refusal cone
Harmless-task evaluation used only 100 random samples from the 14k-question MMLU benchmark due to feasibility/time constraints
LLM-as-judge evaluators can themselves be inaccurate, prone to attacks, or subject to reward hacking, especially for reasoning models with long outputs
quote: while ablating a single direction is insufficient for larger models (e.g., Qwen3 8B and 14B), multiple directions succeed in reducing refusal.
